fields.title: Situation over persona: job stories and the four forces
fields.keyTakeaway: Behavior is explained by the situation, not the persona. And switching to a new solution depends on four forces at once: two push forward, two hold back — and the holding forces are usually stronger because no one thinks about them.
fields.checkQuestion: The product is objectively better, but people aren't using it. Which two forces did you underestimate?
fields.blocks/0/text: The same key question, but from the other angle: **what makes a person change their behavior** — and what stops them.
fields.blocks/1/subtitle: Framing by situation, not by role
fields.blocks/1/items/0: **When** <situation> — the circumstances where the need arises.
fields.blocks/1/items/1: **I want to** <motivation> — what the person is trying to do.
fields.blocks/1/items/3: Difference from a user story: **no role**. A role pushes you to describe the person; a situation pushes you to describe the moment. And decisions are made in the moment.
fields.blocks/2/items/0: “As a cafe owner, I want to see the schedule” — describes a job title
fields.blocks/2/items/1: “When the barista texts in sick on Saturday morning, I want to find a replacement in five minutes so the cafe opens on time” — describes a moment, making the need for speed clear
fields.blocks/3/subtitle: Why people don't switch, even when the new option is better
fields.blocks/3/items/0: **Push from the current solution** — what is frustrating right now. Drives forward.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: **Pull of the new solution** — what makes your solution attractive. Drives forward.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: **Habit** — what holds them back: it works, everyone knows how to use it, no need to change anything.
fields.blocks/3/items/3: **Anxiety** — fear that the new solution will fail: data will be lost, colleagues won't understand, things will get worse.
fields.blocks/4/text: Product teams almost always focus only on the pull of the new solution: adding features. But the sum of forces can remain negative because anxiety and habit haven't been addressed — so no matter how much you add, the switch doesn't happen.
fields.blocks/5/text:
Push: recalculating hours manually, risk of errors.
Pull: automated tracking, schedule visibility.
Habit: the spreadsheet has worked for three years, everyone knows how to use it.
Anxiety: “what if employees don't see the schedule and don't show up?”

For six months, the team kept boosting the pull — adding features. Few switched.

What worked was something else: a “read receipt” for the schedule and the option to run the spreadsheet in parallel for the first month. That addressed anxiety and habit, rather than piling on features.
fields.blocks/6/text: Forces cannot be measured directly — they are reconstructed from interviews about a specific case of switching or refusing to switch. And the model describes the decision to change solutions; it says nothing about whether the person will continue using the product long-term.
